common_name: Mary Todd Daylily (Classic Ruffled Canary-Yellow Daylily)

planting.note: Set bare-root divisions in spring or early fall with the crown just below soil level in full sun and well-drained soil.

directions: Registered by Elmer Claar in 1967, Mary Todd became one of the most widely grown mid-century daylilies for its large, heavily ruffled, clear canary-yellow blooms held on sturdy scapes above tidy foliage clumps. Plant divisions in average, well-drained garden soil and water regularly the first season to establish; established clumps are drought-tolerant and need only occasional division every four to six years to maintain vigorous bloom. Its dependable, long midseason flowering window and exceptional garden toughness kept it in wide commercial and home-garden circulation for decades, making it a benchmark yellow against which later ruffled cultivars were compared.

common_name: Frans Hals Daylily (Historic Bronze-Orange Bicolor Daylily)

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring or fall in full sun; this old, rugged cultivar tolerates poor soil and neglect better than most modern hybrids.

directions: Registered in 1955, Frans Hals is one of the oldest daylily cultivars still commonly sold today, prized for its striking bitone blooms of burnt-orange petals contrasting with mahogany-red sepals. It thrives with minimal care in ordinary garden soil, spreading readily into dense, weed-suppressing clumps that rebloom sporadically through summer once established. Its exceptional hardiness and historic status as a foundation cultivar in daylily breeding make it a favorite for naturalized plantings, roadside beds, and gardeners seeking heirloom perennials with proven multi-generational performance.

common_name: Barbara Mitchell Daylily (Award-Winning Pale Pink Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this cultivar is one of the most extensively propagated daylilies in commerce.

directions: Hybridized by Franklin and Curt Hardy and awarded the Stout Silver Medal in 1993, Barbara Mitchell bears large, heavily ruffled, pale pastel-pink blooms with a deeper pink watermark eye that hold up beautifully in heat and humidity. Grow it in enriched, well-drained soil and divide congested clumps every few years to sustain heavy flowering. Because of its exceptional flower substance, vigor, and near-universal garden performance, it became one of the best-selling and most widely tissue-cultured daylily cultivars of its era, and it remains a standard-bearer for the modern pink daylily class.

common_name: Little Grapette Daylily (Popular Miniature Grape-Purple Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; its compact habit makes it ideal for edging and small-space borders.

directions: Bred by Pauline Henry and registered in 1985, Little Grapette produces abundant small, grape-purple blooms with a green throat on compact, grassy foliage clumps, making it one of the most widely grown miniature daylilies ever introduced. Plant it in average, well-drained garden soil and it will form dense, floriferous clumps that need division only every several years. Its diminutive size, heavy bud count, and reliable performance across a wide climate range have made it a mainstay for rock gardens, mixed borders, and container plantings alike.

common_name: Beverly Sills Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal Ruffled Pink Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, just at or slightly below soil level, in late summer to early fall in full sun with excellent drainage.

directions: Hybridized by Ben Hager and named for the famed opera soprano, Beverly Sills earned the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 1985 for its ruffled, coral-pink blooms with a delicate orange beard. Plant rhizomes with tops exposed to sun in lean, sharply drained soil, since standing moisture and organic mulch against the rhizome invite rot. It has remained one of the most popular and widely propagated tall bearded iris cultivars for decades, valued for its clear pastel color, vigorous increase, and reliable performance across a broad range of climates.

common_name: Dusky Challenger Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal Deep Purple Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and sharply drained soil.

directions: Hybridized by Schreiner's Iris Gardens and awarded the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 1992, Dusky Challenger is a towering tall bearded iris with velvety, near-black deep purple blooms and exceptional bud count and branching. Grow it in full sun with lean, well-drained soil, planting rhizomes shallowly so the tops are not buried, and divide crowded clumps every three to four years. It is widely regarded as one of the most influential and best-selling dark bearded iris cultivars ever released, and it remains a parent behind many modern black-toned iris introductions.

common_name: Jesse's Song Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal White-and-Violet Plicata Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and well-drained soil.

directions: Bred by Bunny Williamson and awarded the Dykes Medal in 1990, Jesse's Song is a classic plicata-pattern tall bearded iris with crisp white petals stitched and stippled in violet-purple around the ruffled edges. Plant rhizomes shallowly in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, and avoid mulching directly over the rhizome to prevent rot. Its crisp bicolor patterning and strong garden vigor made it an enduringly popular exhibition and landscape cultivar, and it is still frequently recommended decades after its introduction as an entry point into collecting plicata-type bearded iris.

common_name: White Swirl Siberian Iris (Historic Ruffled White Siberian Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light shade; established clumps tolerate boggy soil better than bearded iris.

directions: Introduced by hybridizer Steve Varady in 1957, White Swirl was one of the first modern Siberian iris cultivars bred for large, ruffled, pure-white flowers with a bold yellow signal, and it remains a benchmark parent behind many later white Siberian introductions. Plant divisions in humus-rich, evenly moist soil, where clumps of narrow grassy foliage form tidy, self-supporting mounds that need dividing only every four to five years. Unlike bearded iris, it tolerates damp soil and even shallow standing water, making it a long-favored choice for pond margins, rain gardens, and mixed perennial borders.
